Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister, for the Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved the second reading of Bill No. 90 to amend the Government Annuities Act.
He said: The hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Gordon) is absent from the -house attending the meeting of a committee. In view of that fact, coupled with the fact that the purpose of this bill is chiefly to carry out a departmental recommendation with respect to annuities, I venture on his behalf to move the second reading of this bill.
The house is familiar with the history of government annuities. The late Sir Richard Cartwright gave the matter a great deal of personal attention. Originally it was intended that the Government Annuities Act should provide for persons of small means who would secure an annuity for their old age. Gradually and later there came an increase in the amount that might be payable under the statute until at the last the present maximum of $5,000 was fixed. In view of the fact that the government itself defrays the costs of administration, and the rate of interest upon which computations jwith respect to annuities are made is -four per cent-which, as the house knows, is a very high rate-it has been suggested in many quarters that the fund is hardly solvent, because with the prolonging of life consequent upon modern scientific knowledge being applied to diet and hygiene, it is obvious that the old time computations of the period during which an assured might live must be based upon a lower interest rate than four per cent, which is the figure that has been used dn connection with our annuity tables. Therefore the actuaries of the department, having gone over the matter roughly, are satisfied that we should not carry so large an annuity as $5,000 without making an amendment of our rates. That, of course, is undesirable, and so the suggestion by those who have the responsibility for administration-from the standpoint of pure administration apart from policy -is that $1,200 would be a reasonable maximum.
There is another reason that has come to light recently and one I am sure the house will appreciate is a sufficient cause for action being taken. Under the statute making provision for the payment of these annuities it is provided that they are not liable to seizure for the debts of the annuitant, and there are not. lacking illustrations and inci
Annuities Act

dents during the last few years in which fairly well-to-do traders have utilized the funds of their business for the purpose of acquiring an annuity that enabled them to live in comparative ease while their creditors found themselves unable to attach the moneys or use them for the purpose of receiving payment of their debts. Taking the matter all in all, the officials are of the opinion that [DOT]81,200 is a reasonable sum for us to carry under the circumstances and more in keeping with the purposes for which the statute was originally passed.
I move the second reading of the bill standing in the name of the minister, and if it is desired that it should be sent to a committee for the purpose of enabling representations to be made and more detailed discussion to be held, I am perfectly willing after the bill has passed the second reading to make a motion that it be sent to the committee on 'banking and commerce.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to hear the concluding remarks of the Prime Minister that he is willing to send this bill to the committee on banking and commerce, because I think it is a very important measure. I am confident that no member on this side of the house will be opposed to the bill. As the Prime Minister said, the original act was introduced by Sir Richard Cartwright, and I believe the maximum annuity at that time was fixed at $600; subsequently the maximum was increased to $1,000, and then Sir Henry Drayton raised it to $5,000 in 1920. When introducing his amendment Sir Henry said that its main purpose was to secure some extra money at a reduced rate of interest. 1 do not think it is fair to let the impression go abroad that the annuity system is losing money. It may be that it is being administered at a loss, under the present scheme but it must not be forgotten that the revenue derived from the premiums is placed in the consolidated revenue fund and therefore earns no interest. I think to-day there is standing to the credit of the annuities branch in the neighbourhood of $25,000,000. If that money were set aside and drawing interest at five per cent it would produce an annual income of $1,250,000; if we allow for the four per cent the government applies to the money invested, amounting to about $1,000,000, there would still be $250,000 to the credit of the fund each year. Last year I think the administration expenses of the annuities branch, including commissions, advertising, and travelling expenses, amounted to only $111,000, which would still leave a credit balance of $139,000.

I have looked over these figures hurriedly, but if that be the case it seems to me it is hardly fair to suggest that the annuity branch has been run at a loss.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that.

I am speaking more particularly of statements made in the other house and of certain propaganda, which I am certain has been instigated by a few of the large insurance companies. While Minister of Labour I considered the curtailment of the sale of annuities at the maximum of $5,000. In fact it was upon my recommendation that the department cut down the commission on large annuities in order to discourage canvassers running after wealthy men to sell them these large annuities. In this way I think we effected some curtailment of the sale of the larger annuities. That is one reason why I think the government of the day ought not hastily to have introduced this amendment, but rather to have Waited until they had decided on a well-defined system in regard to the annuities branch. It was my view, and I recall the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) making the statement some time ago, that the annuities branch could well be extended so as to take in old age pensions, unemployment insurance and other insurance of a social character. I find that of the 1,772 annuity contracts 1,482, or 83-6 per cent, are for $600 ; 212, or 12 per cent are from $601 to $1,200; 38, or 2-2 per cent are from $1,201 to $1,500. In fact only nine of them are between $2,501 and $5,000.
Is that the total number of annuities to which we are now obligated, or is that the total number for the last year?

That is the total number in existence altogether. The point I want to make is this: Inasmuch as there are not very many wealthy men, comparatively speaking, taking advantage of this opportunity, we might have deferred amending the act until such time as the government made up its mind what it will do with respect to social insurance of all kinds. However, it may be that even yet some recommendation will be made in committee which may lead the government of the day to change its mind with respect to the bill. .

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
have just a word to say. First of all I wish to express the hope that the Prime Minister will adopt the course which he has suggested, namely, that of referring this measure to one of the select standing committees. I assume it will be to the committee on industrial and international relations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, the committee on
banking and commerce, I should think; it is a financial matter.

I had rather
hoped it might be considered by the committee on industrial and international relations, which would be in a position to examine the measure in its relation to the social problems of the day. My thought has been for some years past, as the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Ileenan) has just mentioned, that the an-anuities scheme which was started many years ago by this parliament might be broadened out into a scheme of social insurance generally, to be administered by the federal administration, and that as such it might prove to be an important factor in helping to solve many of the social problems of the day.
When the Annuities Act was introduced, some doubt was expressed as to the advantage which would be taken of a measure of that kind. The statistics of the department now prove conclusively that the people of Canada generally are appreciative of legislation of the kind, whereby through making a certain contribution themselves towards unforeseen contingencies, the state is placed in a position to protect them in a time of emergency. Annuities soon become a form of old age insurance, and as such are of service to the state as well as to the individual, in the relief they afford in times of need to those who are of advanced years. If the Annuities Act performs a service in that regard, it seems to me the measure might be broadened out to include all forms of social insurance, as for example, insurance against accident or sickness or invalidity, as well as dependency in old age, in all of which ways it would serve a very great social purpose. It might, too,
be made to become the means whereby unemployment insurance at the instance of the federal government would gradually be introduced in this country.
I was going to venture the hope that the government would refer this measure to the committee on industrial and international relations, with an expression of desire that the committee would consider the measure in its bearing upon a larger scheme of social insurance. The reason I believe it is advisable that this should be done immediately is that if the larger scheme were contemplated it would, I believe, be a mistake to reduce the amount which might be contributed by individuals for the purpose of gaining the kind of protection which the measure thus enlarged would afford. I simply make the suggestion as one which I believe will be helpful. If it is not taken advantage of at the moment, I venture the prophecy that some day not far distant it will become a part of the social legislation of the government of the day.

I am opposed to the second reading of this measure. I am of the opinion that the Prime Minister is doing a wise thing in suggesting that it be referred to a committee for further consideration. I hope the committee will see fit to amend it so as to restore the old condition. If the principle of government annuities is correct; if it is a sound principle-and I believe in it myself-I see no reason under heaven why it should be limited to men who are able to subscribe to the extent of securing an annuity of $1,200 a year or $100 a month. I do not see why the people in this country who want to take out annuities of from $2,000 to $5,000 should not have that privilege. However, I do agree that as far as it is possible any system of annuity should be made self-supporting, and if there are any amendments to be made either in connection with the terms of t'he contracts or the rates to be paid in order to make the whole scheme self-supporting, I am in accord with the view that this should be done.
I do not wish to discuss the matter further at this time, except to say that I regard the proposal coming from the other chamber as a reactionary one, calculated to be of more direct benefit to the private insurance companies of Canada than to the common people of the country. I look upon it as an evasion of government responsibility in connection with social insurance of every kind, or at least a modification of that responsibility, and I deeply regret the moving of this bill at all. If it had been in the form of a change
Annuities Act

in the rates or something of that kind, I could have sympathized with it and understood it, but it deliberately goes back to a rate of $1,200 instead of a maximum of $5,000, which I think is a retrogade step and one which will chiefly help the life insurance companies.

Mr. Speaker, I think there is a good deal in what the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has just stated. For my part, I agree with the Prime Minister on one point, that regard should be had to the current changes in the rates of interest, but on the other hand I also remember one of the most valuable suggestions made in this chamber some years ago by the z-ight hon. gentleman himself, when sitting on this side of the house. He then pointed out the advantage that would accrue to the government, to the public generally and to the clients of insurance companies should the government force the great insurance companies to invest a large proportion of their funds in government securities. Encouraging private citizens to take insurance directly with the government instead of with the insurance companies induces the public to invest their money for long terms with the government of the country. In this way the public can help sustain the public credit of the country.
With regard to the rate of interest, of course there is something to be said, but there is also this to be kept in mind, that the government do not have to pay all the charges supported by the private companies. They have not the same rentals for offices; they do not pay insurance on their buildings; they do not pay dividends to shareholders. The government thereby save a large proportion of the so-called fixed charges in connection with the management of these funds, and that is also the case in connection with the post office savings bank and other government administrative departments.
The observations of the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) and of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) should also be taken into consideration. This is the only form of insurance so far carried by the government, but ultimately it will become the nucleus of the various forms of social insurances which the government will have to take over and operate before long. Whether we like it or not, we have to face conditions as they present themselves, in this or in any other country. Some forty or fifty years ago Sir William Vernon Harcourt, then chancellor of the exchequer, being charged with a tendency to socialism, replied, "I hate 
socialism but we are forced into it whether we like it or not." Well, this government has been forced into it, as was the previous government. Before making any change in this matter I think some consideration should be given to the future.
There is another point on which I agree with the Prime Minister. I refer to a more recent statement of his. At the beginning of the session he said, rightly I think, that the spirit of speculation was one of the causes of the present economic distress not only in Canada but in other countries as well. He was taken to task by hon. members to my left, and perhaps he made a mistake in connecting that statement a little too closely with the situation in the western provinces. But broadly speaking, he was absolutely right. The spirit of speculation is the curse of our times in Canada as well as in other countries.
Now, the establishment of insurance of this kind on a long term scale, postponing the reaping of sums invested with the government, is an inducement to people to save and is also a safeguard against speculation. It seems to me that we have a sufficient number of men of wealth, or at least men of fair means, who instead of throwing money into all sorts of wildcat schemes should be encouraged to invest with the government at a moderate rate of interest, and in such a way as not to get their money back until their old age, when they are supposed to be wiser, and before they become a charge upon the public. I do not think there is any necessity for restricting the limit of this insurance.
With regard to rates, that should be revised properly, bearing in mind what I have said as to the possible enlargement of administration. Once we have created various forms of social insurance under the management of the federal government, then the administration of all these departments will naturally curtail the proportion of expenditure carried by each of the departments. Secondly, I would make this suggestion to the government. It seems to me that it would be more proper and more in accordance with the present state of things in Canada, as well as with the spirit that should govern in these matters, that a limit should be defined as to the margin of these annuities which shall be exempt from income tax. I understand that at the present time any annuity paid by the government is exempt from income tax. Suppose the government brought in an amendment limiting the exemption from income tax to the sum of $1,200, and bringing under the operation of the Income Tax Act any surplus that might accrue. For example, an annuity of $3,000 would be exempt up to

Annuities Act
$1,200, but would come under the Income Tax Act at $1,800, and so on. That would establish a difference between the small annuitants, the labourer or the man of small means, and the man with a larger income.
A man of small means who had been able to invest any surplus over and above what was absolutely necessary to sustain him in his old age would continue to be exempt up to a certain point; but the man with the larger income would still be invited to invest his money with the government. He might take out a moderate or even a large annuity, but upon everything over and above $1,200 he would have to pay income tax in proportion to the amount of the annuity.
It seems to me that, taking all these things together, the department being considered the nucleus of a social insurance branch; the great advantage which the government has over private concerns in the maintenance of a little higher rate of interest; and the general advantage from all points of view, economic and social, of inviting men of large or small means to invest their money with the government in order indirectly to carry on the affairs of the country, instead of investing it in all sorts of speculation-taking all these things into consideration, I say, the government would be wise in not diminishing the amount of money which might be invested in annuities, but in making a certain proportion of the annuities subject to income tax.
I should like to correct the figures I gave a little while ago in answer to the hon. member for Bow River and the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The hon. member will do so with the consent of the house.
He is merely making a correction.

In order to have the record correct, I may say that the number of contracts in force on March 31, 1930, was as follows: immediate, 4,012; deferred, 6,171; or a total of 10,183. The amount of such annuities was $3,893,122.73. The amount^ received on account of the purchase of annuities from September 1, 190S, to March 31, 1930, exclusive of amounts returned to purchasers, was S24,860,087.95. The number of annuities sold last year, between $2,501 and $5,000, was 9.

I should regret to see this bill in its present form become law; it would be certainly a retrograde step for parliament to sanction it as it stands. This would apply to joint annuities, and a limit of $1,200 a year is not sufficient. We hope that
the majority of our people will be able tt enjoy a larger annuity than that when they come to those years in which they must give up active work. I submit that it is wrong in principle to sanction the change proposed^ in this bill, and unless something is done to improve it, I certainly think it should be opposed on the third reading.
I believe the Prime Minister stated that the present basis of annuities was not actuarially sound.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before the motion is put I should like to make two or three observations. There appears to me to be some misapprehension on the part of some hon. gentlemen opposite. The ex-iMinister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) said that there were 4,000 outstanding, presently payable annuities. That means that 4,000 separate sums of money have been paid for the purpose of securing annuities payable from the date of the taking-out of such annuities until death or until a fixed period of time, that is, say the age of seventy, or whatever age may be decided upon. That would mean that out of the entire 10,000. two-fifths or 40 per cent were payments made to secure present annuities. The annuities are based upon two considerations, the earning power of money and the expectation of life. The earning power of money is a matter of prime concern at the moment only in so far as it affects the present payments, font one has to look into the future to ascertain whether or not that presently contemplated rate of interest can be continued over the period ot the expectation of life. It is just because of that single fact that this bill is before this house at the present time, for that and no other reason.
When Sir Richard Cartwright instituted annuities he provided for a maximum of $50 per month or $600 per year. Any hon. gentlemen who are interested can read what the purposes of the government were in placing this amount at $600 per annum to be paid at old age or otherwise, as the annuitant might elect. The reasons why that small sum was fixed upon are explained by Sir Richard Cartwright himself.
Annuities Act

The hon. member (Mr. Heenan) has explained very naively why the amount was increased at one particular period in this country's history. It did secure more money, in fact we have to-day some $23,000,000 or $24,000,000 in the treasury which has been paid in by annuitants under contracts by which the Dominion of Canada undertakes to pay presently so much per annum until a given contingency has arrived, or to commence the payments in futurity at the age of 50, 55 or 60 as the case may be. That is based upon this single consideration: that the actuaries were of the opinion that, having regard to the present and future earning power of money, it was safe for the country to make that contract and when the annuitants died or the age limit was reached the money would be exhausted and there would neither be a surplus nor a deficit. That is the science upon which these annuities are worked out.
Two things have supervened; one is the very condition mentioned by the hon. member for Kenora that not only is the annuity exempt from the operations of the income tax but it has become an incentive to some people, such as traders in a small way, who exhaust their resources to obtain some money to buy a presently payable annuity and the rest of their creditors can whistle. That is not fancy, it is a fact. When my hon. friend stated that .the number of present annuities was 4,000 out of a total of 10,000, it will be seen to what extent an effort has been made to buy annuities presently payable.
The reasons why the maximum amount was advanced to $5,000 have been given by the former Minister of Labour, but I am thinking of to-day. One must look into the future and be able to say that beyond peradventure a sum of money paid to-day by an annuitant will at any rate of interest which may be payable for money in the future-the future is the expectation of life-secure the payment of the sum contracted to be paid. As my hon. friend has said, there is no question at all of expenditure, nor is it a matter of moment, but having regard to the conditions to which I have referred no one will say that the rate is one which can with confidence and certainty be looked upon as other than a high rate, having regard to the changes which have taken place in connection with the price of money and the interest which it will earn.
May I put this further consideration to the house because it has become important as the days have gone by: It is not desirable that the rates should be increased in connection with these annuities. Nothing would be more detrimental to the general policy of the gov-
[Mr. Bennett. 1
eminent in granting annuities under this scheme than that the rate should be increased. I need hardly say to as well informed a house as this that in all questions of annuities the rate is determined by almost pure mathematics. There is practically no variation in the rates quoted by the insurance companies, and the government rate would undoubtedly be the same were it not for the fact referred to by my hon. friend, namely, that there was a disposition on the part of parliament when granting an annuity of $600 that the state itself should absorb the expenses-private enterprises make the expenses quite large-but it never was intended that the state should provide annuities on a large scale for those who are well able to take them from private enterprises and pay whatever premium might be demanded. In other words, the net result of the continuance of the rate which originally provided for a $600 annuity, based upon the earning power of .money looking into a long future being four per cent, has been, by increasing the annuity to $5,000, to make it a direct incentive to those who desire to secure the benefits from the state of what was intended for the man of small means. The very fact that 4,000 out of 10,000 annuities are of this class proves my contention.
This is a departmental matter, it is to insure against the necessity of increasing the rates for small annuities; it is to continue the system to which Sir Richard Cartwright gave so much time and attention, and which in my judgment-that does not add anything to it-is founded upon a sound consideration and appreciation of the facts which should govern any body in granting annuities, whether it be a private enterprise or public body. This has nothing to do with social insurance. The time will come when those matters will be considered on a contributary basis, which means that the contribution .made is the premium paid for the insurance granted, whether it be old age insurance, unemployment or invalidity insurance, or whatever it may be. Insurance of any kind involves a premium and the premium must be based upon some consideration of facts and not fancy. We endeavoured in the first instance to base our premium rate upon a due and proper appreciation of the state absorbing certain charges, for the benefit of the man in whom we desired to encourage the habit of thrift, but advantage has been taken of this not only with respect to income tax but otherwise, and the officials of the department have endeavoured to set a rate based upon the scheme which was originally launched

Annuities Act
and to provide an annuity of $1,200 which represents fairly now the $600 which was in the minds of those who put forward the scheme in the first instance. I do not believe that it is desirable to change the rates with respect to those who have secured the benefits of this system in the way of small annuities; it would be wrong; it would be unfair and they would think that there was something wrong with the system.
The hon. member for Kenora is quite right in saying that there is no question of the solvency of the system, nor have the expenses of running the system been very large, but in this, as in life insurance, one must think of the period of time during which the contract will exist, and that period of time is based upon the expectation of life of the annuitant. If my hon. friend misunderstood me I am sorry because all I was endeavouring to show was that in their desire to maintain the solvency of the system itself, the officers charged with responsibility decided after a rough actuarial computation that we should not have increased the annuity to the sum mentioned. It was done as the hon. gentleman has very fairly stated under exceptional circumstances.
I think the committee on banking and commerce is the proper committee to which the bill should go. The question of social insurance will come up in time, but this is a matter of pure mathematics, actuarial computations, and the determination of whether or not a system which was created for the purpose of ensuring a certain amount of confidence in the future on the part of those who had small sums of money, shall not be extended beyond a reasonable sum, namely $1,200, which in these days takes the place of the $600 originally provided for by the act.

I have been trying to agree
with my right hon. friend's whole argument; but if he stated, as I think he did, that actuarially it is desirable that the amount be reduced from $5,000 to $1,200, and if this is entirely a mathematical matter, as it is, why is it not just as desirable so far as the $1,200 is concerned? Would the proper remedy not be to change the rates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
North Waterloo has asked a question such as I would have expected him to ask, a very proper question. The reason is this: The original system was based upon annuities for, shall I say, the thrifty person of small means, and the state then felt that $600 could very well be taken care of without incurring any large expense, and that 4 per cent would probably
be a rate that would always be serviceable to the state. That was the general view taken of the matter. The officers of the department say that to-day $1,200 may well be regarded as the maximum sum that will take the place of $600 which was the maximum at that time. Actuarially they are practically on the same basis. I have told the hon. member that the principle that governed the creation of the system in the first instance is still to be maintained while the rate is to be continued. The payment of annuity costs, by the state is the slight contribution the state makes to the system for the purpose of encouraging thrift.
Not to take care of the man who is able to take care of himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Is there in this bill anything which will prevent employers of labour from taking out annuities for their employees?

speechtext:
There is no change in
any particular and employers of labour will still, I hope and believe, avail themselves of this legislation for that very purpose.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Minister of Marine) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize a loan to the harbour commissioners of Halifax in an amount not exceeding $3,500,000 for the construction of terminal facilities, upon approval by the governor in council of detailed plans, specifications and estimates for such works, and the deposit of the debentures of the corporation to cover said loan.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
Has the minister before him a list of the proposed works contemplated by this particular vote?

The new works to be started this season according to the estimates consist of thirteen small items amounting to only $386,000. This amount of $3,500,000 is to provide for those new works estimated to cost about $386,000 and also the -continuation of works which were authorized during the term of the late government. According to the estimates made by our engineers, the amount necessary to complete the works authorized by the late government is $2,728,384. When the new commissioners took office last September they learned that some works which had been started had not been authorized by the government. However we could do nothing but continue those works, because they were so far advanced, and also in order to relieve unemployment. The result is that another amount of $385,000 is required to terminate the unauthorized works which had been begun before the new commission came into office. There is also expenditure to be made for pier No. 5 over and above the amount of the contract. As the committee knows, there are two piers under construction at the present time, pier B and pier 5. We had to stop work on pier 5 on account of the fact that the contractors were not building it according to the plans and specifications, and on account of the further -fact that the specifications were not complete and there was danger of the structure being destroyed. Now we are contemplating calling for new tenders for a more complete pier, which will necessitate an increased expenditure of $288,000. It was found that the width of pier B, 260 feet, was absolutely inadequate to take care of two berths and railroad facilities. Therefore our engineers had to increase the width to 300 feet, which will necessitate an increased expenditure of $178,000 in round figures. Then, too, in the first estimates no provision had been made for contingencies and for interest on capital expenditure during construction; the amount necessary to look after these is estimated at $534,000. It will be seen that the sum of $3,500,000 is absolutely necessary to complete the work which was started before the present administration took office. This total includes also $3S6,000 to provide for certain work to be done this season in order to put the -wharf in such condition that it may be used. I shall be pleased to give any -further details that may be required when the bill is before the house.

What does the minister mean when he says certain works were unauthorized? Does he mean that the plans and specifications had not been produced to the department for approval; or that certain work which had been started was continued after the appropriation was exhausted; or that work was undertaken on the initiative of the harbour commissioners themselves?

The works were started by the late commissioners on their own initiative without any authorization, although they contended that they had had some conversation with the minister of the department and the engineers and thought they had been authorized verbally, but this was denied by the officials. Therefore we contend that these works were started absolutely on the initiative of the late commissioners.
Halifax Harbour

I understand that the
minister has not before him all the details, and I should not like to embarrass him at this stage in any way at all. But is he in a position to tell the committee if the works which were started by the late commissioners on their own initiative were works in regard to the general development of the harbour of Halifax, and were included in the general plan which has been in the department for several years?

If I remember well, the late commissioners contended that they had a general plan for the development of the harbour at a cost of about $16,000,000 and that the amounts authorized by parliament, first, $500,000 and then $5,000,000, were onlj' for the execution of the first part of the large scheme that we have had to modify for the time being.
Is it not a fact that these plans covering the general scheme had been deposited with the Department of Marine for nearly ten years?

I do not know; but I am sure of one thing-the general scheme involving an expenditure of $15,000,000 has never been authorized by the department. There is no document on the files which tends to show any such authorization. The late harbour commissioners may have discussed the matter with the deputy minister, and they may have shown their general scheme to him, but there never was an authorization by the department to go ahead and incur those expenditures.

I should not like to contradict the minister, but I am under the impression that the general scheme for the development of the port of Halifax, necessitating the expenditure of many millions of dollars, had already been approved by the department, but had not been put into effect. Do I understand the minister to say the late commissioners when they started the work on their own initiative contributed a certain amount of the expenditure out of the harbour revenues, or are all the accounts for those works due at the present time?

When we came into power I think the harbour commissioners were overdrawn to the extent of about $1,500,000. We helped them out as much as we could in order to continue the works which were under construction.

This resolution, Mr. Chairman, is to authorize a loan of $3,500,000 to the harbour commissioners of Halifax, and they are to deposit their debentures to guar-

antee the loan. Do I understand that they have to pay interest to the government on the loans?

Of course all loans to harbour commissions bear interest. Some of the harbour commissions cannot pay interest because they have not sufficient revenue for the purpose. This loan will be advanced progressively during the construction of the work and no doubt it will bear interest. Whether the harbour commission of Halifax will be able to pay the interest only the future will disclose.
Then they cannot pay interest on this loan unless they collect dues on the boats which will use the harbour facilities; that is their only source of revenue?
They pay interest out of their revenues after they have paid their overhead expenses.

Has not my friend heard of a certain promise, that the harbours of Halifax and St. John were to be what were called national, free ports, and that it was a crime that rates should be charged on goods coming to those ports? Has not my hon. friend heard of such a statement being made at any time by anyone with whom he is related or connected?
I have not heard anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Nor has anyone else.

I know the harbour
commissioners have by-laws by which they collect dues.
This means the end of the free port, the national port?
For the time being.

In order to put the matter properly before the house and have it thoroughly understood let me quote from the speech of the Prime Minister at Halifax on July 3:
Halifax and St. John should be national ports. They, belong to the people of Canada. They should be great, free, open ports.
Then, speaking at St. John, he said:
The port of St. John should be a great free port, a national port, and towards the implementation of this object I give my pledge. It is said that I am opposed to the port of St. John as at present operated. I am opposed to the collection of tolls in this port which prevents it from being built up. _My ambition is to see this port the cheapest in the world.

I did not hear who made that promise.

Halifax Harbour
The present Prime Minister of Canada, then leader of the opposition, on June 30.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What are you quoting from?
I am quoting from the St. John Telegraph and the Halifax Herald.

About a month ago I asked for the production of the order in council appointing Sir Alexander Gibb to make an investigation into all the harbours of Canada. The Prime Minister at the time was not quite sure whether an order in council had been passed or whether Sir Alexander Gibb had been retained through correspondence, but he promised to table the correspondence if there was any. I quite understand that due to the pressure of business he may have forgotten it, so I would ask him to be kind enough to lay on the table of the house a copy of the correspondence and a copy of any order in council which might have been passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite right; I had overlooked it. I looked up the matter, and there is no order in council There was correspondence carried on with the High Commissioner in London, and there were some telephone calls, I think. I will give the substance of it as my memory serves me. First of all there was a cable to have the High Commissioner call upon Sir Alexander Gibb to see if he would be free to accept the retainer. Then there was a reply, after the High Commissioner had seen Sir Alexander Gibb, and a definite agreement that he could send his officials in May and later come himself. There was a telephone call to the High Commissioner to complete the matter, and Sir Alexander Gibb and his officers came out accordingly.

May I ask what were the
instructions given Sir Alexander Gibb?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The instructions were
twofold. First of all he was to ascertain to what extent the existing facilities could be extended and utilized for the purpose of serving the respective territories in which they were situated, especially having regard to the national character of those upon the sea coast. I am speaking from memory now. The second part of the instructions was whether any suggestions could be made as to the manner of administration of the several ports.
Those instructions doubtless were given in writing?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The instructions, if my
memory serves me, were given by the Minister of Marine to the engineers. Sir Alexander expected that he would consider this problem without in any sense having his activities curbed or restrained by a government, and that he would determine how these ports could best be made into national ports in every sense of the term, including Vancouver, St. John, Halifax and, in the summer time, Quebec and Montreal.
And Three Rivers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I had forgotten the hon. member's port. The port of Casgrain also is not overlooked.

If the convention between
members in the other end of the chamber could be carried on in a little louder tone we would be able to get the drift of what is going on, but we cannot hear a word.

Do I understand that the
scope of this investigation does not cover the port of Vancouver?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I said Vancouver. I am
sorry the hon. member did not hear me.

But surely, Mr. Speaker,
some instructions in writing have been given, or there must be a minute of the privy council or something in writing which the house could see, which might be produced on the table of the house, permitting us to understand and fully comprehend what is the commission of Sir Alexander Gibb.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should think he was
instructed in exactly the same manner as Mr. Frederick Palmer was instructed; he was asked to come out and report upon these harbours. I think there is a written minute, not of council, but which the Minister of Marine has, with respect to the two matters into which he was to inquire. If you employ technical men it is not wise to endeavour to circumscribe their activities, and this gentleman is regarded as one of the foremost in his profession. He has been asked to report upon these ports, having regard to the two points which I have already mentioned and which I need not repeat. In no sense has it been suggested to him the particular part of the harbour at which he should look, or the particular way in which he should consider it. He is to consider it from the standpoint of a Canadian national activity.

In that respect you gave
him a free hand?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Exactly.

The circumstances are not
quite the same as those under which the
Halifax Harbour

gentleman referred to by the Prime Minister came to Canada. He was asked to decide on the respective merits of two ports. Sir Alexander Gibb, as I understand it, was asked to come here and generally recommend to the government what position should be taken, or what policy should be followed, with regard to the ports on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and on the St. Lawrence. He is not instructed further than to tell the government what they should do. Will the Prime Minister tell me if I am correct in that statement? His job, in other words, is to devise a policy for the government; is that it? I am asking the question without endeavouring to insinuate that the government is not capable of carrying on, but I should like the Prime Minister to give me some kind of an answer to what I think is a very reasonable question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The policy of the administration will be settled when it is in possession of the information which Sir Alexander Gibb will furnish. In the meantime, with a free hand he is to look over the physical conditions and report upon that plan which, in his judgment, will best insure-as I think I mentioned to my colleague-continuous development of the ports in question, looking forward for twenty-five to fifty years.

I am sure every member of this house, and particularly those interested in maritime matters, will approve of the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister, but is it not a fact that the question of freedom from dues is something which, after all, should be a matter of policy of the government? If that is the case, I am assuming that Sir Alexander Gibb will advise the government as to whether or not these ports are to be free. I wonder whether the Prime Minister will take his advice if he says that these ports, in order to maintain their staff and to carry on their business, must impose certain tonnage dues, moorage charges, wharfage and so on. If the Prime Minister is not prepared to follow his advice and to take his counsel on matters of this importance, I wonder what the usefulness of Sir Alexander Gibb is and why he has been brought here at all. I might ask the Prime Minister to tell us what he had in mind when he urged so strenuously during the last election that these ports should be free. Did he mean that they should be free from customs dues or free from tolls?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman were always serious it would not be so difficult to answer him; it would be much

easier, I daresay. Surely he does not seriously think that they would be free from customs duties.
The only known free ports in the world are ports which are free of customs duties, such as Hamburg. That is the meaning of the term.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not the meaning of the term.
In the mind of the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not the meaning in which the term has been used. It has been properly pointed out that the harbour of Quebec has made no payment of interest to the government on the enormous expenditures that have been made, which expenditures have been used very largely under the auspices of my hon. friend, for purposes largely political. And it was felt that perhaps the time had come when an effort should be made to lift the administration out of politics. As regards the harbour of Halifax, if it is desired to discuss again what transpired there before the last election, that will be done. But the matter at the moment is sub judice and we will leave it at that.
That is not an answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am coming to the answer. I am wondering whether the hon. gentleman wishes it.
That is a nice way to avoid it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not avoiding it. I still say that I have an ambition that these Atlantic ports should be free, and I mean just what I said: free ports where ships can come and go without paying tolls. That is exactly what I meant.
Does the right hon. gentleman know of any port in the world which is free in that sense?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I certainly do. Hamburg is a free port-
It is not free in that sense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know of his own knowledge?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Who told him?
From having read every dictionary in the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Dictionaries are not the
source of information to which one should go

Halifax Harbour
to find out what the situation is in the port of Hamburg. I took the trouble to inquire
of a gentleman who transacts business in that port. He may have been misinformed, but he told me what was meant by a free port. And the meaning of the term is as I have stated. The term free port means free of tolls, and I still have an ambition that these ports may be free of tolls. The money has been expended and they cannot possibly pay interest on the investment made. I do not think the house listened with as much attention as possibly the country will to the statement of what took place in Halifax before the last election with respect to the expenditure of moneys. The Minister of Marine pointed out that contracts had been made, and when I hear hon. gentlemen opposite talk about parliamentary control and authority, it vastly amuses me to recall the exact record of what transpired a few months before the last election in connection with the harbours of Halifax and St. John. We are not discussing St. John to-day, but when the time comes I shall read to the house a letter written by the ex-Postmaster General with respect to that harbour. It is interesting reading in the light of subsequent events.

Do you mean that as a
threat?
No, a promise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Exactly, a promise.

Do you think I am afraid
of it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not suggest the
hon. gentleman would be.

I am prepared to meet the
right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Very well; I will meet
my hon. friend at Philippi. Now, it might be desirable to get away from politics in discussing these harbours.
Who started it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is easily known who
did.
The Prime Minister did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When?

The Prime Minister went
out of his way to allege that there had been some political activity in the port of Quebec, simply because I asked him a straight, honest question, which he wished to avoid. If he wants to talk politics in relation to Quebec harbour, I will do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot restrain the
hon. gentleman-

He may investigate the
harbour until he is blue in the face, but if he will give me an investigation into the last ten months as compared with the ten years previous, I am willing at any time to have such an investigation made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Now that the hon. gentleman has made that statement, I hope he feels better. I was merely observing that it would advance the interest of the ports to avoid acrimonious political discussion.
Why did you start it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The records are there,
with respect to Halifax, St. John and Quebec. Let us hope that out of these vast sums that have been expended we may be able to create ports that will be of some service to the Canadian people. At the moment we are discussing the harbour of Halifax, and the grant of $3,500,000 in connection therewith. That involves questions with respect to the report of Sir Alexander Gibb in reference to that harbour and to others as well.
The ex-Minister of Justice asked a question with regard to the term "free" in relation to the ports of Halifax and St. John. I explained exactly what was meant by that word when I made statements in both Halifax and St. John, and it will be found that I said, free from tolls of every kind. And I still believe that these harbours should be free if we are to make them the national asset we should like; because, in the winter, this country's grain must pass through them if it is not to pass through the port of a foreign country. They must be free if we are to compete successfully with ports that have been heavily subsidized in one way or another, and in some instances, in a foreign country, by Canadian money. In connection with our own railway systems, we have abandoned our efforts-and properly so-in a neighbouring state, and are now devoting ourselves to two ports in our own country. And we are doing so not for a local but for a national purpose, in order that the grain, not moved out of the great lakes in the fall of the year, may find access to the markets of the world at the lowest possible rate. And this applies not only to grain but to other commodities as well, both outgoing and incoming. It is one of my ambitions, if I have any-and I confess to having few- that these harbours should be free ports, and I have given some attention to them in that sense.
One of the matters I took up with my colleague at the earliest opportunity after coming back from England was the question of securing the services of an eminent authority

Halifax Harbour

to report upon these ports, because I felt that we should adopt something in the nature of the plan that prevails in Southampton, or the port of London authority, or the port of Liverpool. The port of Liverpool commission is independent, and in Southampton their operations are based upon a plan made years ago. In other words, our plan looks to a gradual, steady and continuous development over perhaps half a century. What I did suggest in connection with the work of Sir Alexander Gibb, whom I have not seen personally, was that this work might be carried on looking towards a development over a period of half a century-culminating not today or to-morrow, and involving the expenditure not merely of a million or two million dollars, providing a port suitable for immediate necessities, but looking to the long future. It was on that basis that he was asked to make his report. I do not know whether a quarter of a century or half a century was mentioned, but it was certainly a long period of years. We look forward to a development such as has taken place at Southampton, affording room for expansion as necessity may arise. At Southampton, for instance, in connection with the work commenced last year, they are looking to the provision of facilities for the accommodation of a ship of 1,000 feet, the new Cunard boat. That is one of the things they are already doing. I had hoped that, so far as these ports of ours are concerned, we might be able to treat them in that way, so that as our development expanded we might be able, without scrapping what had already been accomplished, to plan for further growth within a period of forty or fifty years. Town planning is carried on with a general conception of the needs of community, and these harbours should be built upon a similar plan. When as a young man I first went to London that port was not regarded as having the facilities of, say, the port of Liverpool, but the port of London, notably under the chairmanship of the late Lord Davenport, became a wonderful place. The character of the work carried on there is beyond any description which could be made by an hon. member of this house in a few minutes. I look forward to something of that sort in respect to these harbours. Enormous sums of money have been expended on the harbour of Montreal, but this is neither the time nor the place to discuss what in my judgment has imperilled that port; this can be discussed at another time. On the Pacific coast we have Vancouver and New Westminster. Every hon. member knows exactly what has happened at New Westminster;

we have either to find $300,000 or the elevator will topple over the brink. New Westminster has not paid its interest charges, but it is not charging tolls. Vancouver has paid interest on its securities. Whether or not we can develop these ports to the extent which we would like and charge tolls, I cannot at the moment say. That is still my ambition and I shall endeavour as far as I can to secure its realization. This is all I can usefully say with respect to these matters.

Mr. Chairman, leaving aside for the moment the question of free ports, I must comment upon the right hon. gentleman deliberately going out of his way to point the finger of scorn at the haifoour of Quebec. That harbour is not (paying its interest, but I do not believe the harbours of Halifax or St. John are paying their interest. My right hon. friend might have mentioned those harbours while he was at it. Perhaps Vancouver is paying its interest, but the Prime Minister tells us that he wishes the day to come when none of these harbours will be obliged to pay interest charges and that they will not have to exact any tolls or moorage charges from the shipping of Canada. If that is his ambition, and he says it is, I do not see why he attaches any blame to those harbours which have not the revenue and are not likely ever to have the revenue sufficient to pay their way. I think it has been the policy of every government and of every party in this country for many years to develop these ports as national ports. Coming back to the question of free ports, any dictionary or encyclopaedia will indicate that a free port is nothing more or less than a bonded warehouse. The free port of Hamburg and such others are ports in which goods come from all over the world to foe held without the payment of customs duty until such time as they are taken out.

Mr. Chairman, I have
knocked around the world a lot
Much more than have I.

I was brought up in a maritime province where we had shipping sailing all over the world, and I always heard the mariners say that such and such a place is a free port, meaning that there were no port dues exacted with respect to entry of shipping sailing to or from that port. It is a common expression among mariners.

Will the hon. gentleman
name one?	,
There are many of them.

Which ones?

Halifax Harbour
There certainly used to be in my younger days.
I can name one, the port of Riviere du Loup.

When we were discussing this matter before I raised a question with the former Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin). I stated that Quebec would never be able to pay the interest upon the bonds then outstanding and the further bonds to be issued. The former minister said that he had in view the development of a scheme to make Quebec a free port in that sense, and he made a promise to the house to that effect. I remember that statement being made when criticism was-
I never promised a free port.

No hon. member in this
house and no one out of the house ever understood the right hon. leader of the government, when speaking of free ports, to mean ports which would be free from customs duties.
I know that.

My hon. friend has

We understood what the right hon. gentleman meant. I do
Halifax Harbour

not pretend to know now, but I daresay X can find port after port which in the last twenty-five years has been made free from port and harbour dues to vessels entering and leaving. I have discussed, not in St. John, but in Halifax, with a number of merchants the question of Halifax being a port which would be free from port dues of that kind, that is, wharfage and harbour dues. That idea has never been prevalent in Halifax and I doubt if it was ever prevalent in St. John. I doubt if the words used by the Prime Minister could have been interpreted in that sense, and when I was using the word "nonsense," I thought it was nonsensical to give that meaning to the terms used by him.
My hon. friend did not understand what was said.

I think my hon. friend is

Free ports. A term applied to ports, or more usually zones within ports, in which vessels can load and unload, and commercial and even manufacturing businesses can be carried on, without any active control by the fiscal authorities.
Is that nonsensical, I ask my hon. friend? I find it in the Encyclopaedia Britannica. The author of this must have travelled all over the world and had some experience, so I hope my hon. friend will not say that he was saying something nonsensical. The article continues:

I commend that to the Prime Minister.

And so on.
Merchandise can be brought into the free port free of duty and customs examination, and stored, repacked, sorted, etc., at will, and then either reshipped or sent into Germany as the conditions of the market may suggest. Before the resolution

subtopic: CENTRALIZED CONTROL OF EXPENDITURE BY NEW OFFICIAL TO BE KNOWN AS COMPTROLLER OF THE TREASURY

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 102, to amend the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when the bill was introduced I promised to make an explanation to the house of the provisions of the proposed measure. The existing Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act has been on the

Revenue and Audit Act
statute books since 1878 practically in its present form. In fact, if the wording of the act of that year is compared with that of the present act it will be found to be almost identical, and if the curious will look back to the British act of 1866 he will there find the origin of our present statute.
Of course it is a far cry from 1878 to the present time, and during that period many changes have been introduced in accounting, largely because of the increase in volume. In 1930 the business of this country amounted in one month to practically the whole or more than the whole volume of business in 1878. It therefore involves, of course, much more work and, I think, a much more complicated form of accounting because of the size of the country and the fact that the population, sparse as it is, is scattered over a vast area.
The officers of the Department of Finance have, as a matter of fact, been engaged for some time-before the advent to power of this government-in an endeavour to deal with the problems of accounting. In the last few months a very earnest effort has been made to coordinate the activities of all those who have been engaged in this work, and the result has been that a measure has been drafted which was circulated to the heads of the several departments; and after much consideration, the elimination of a proposed section here and the addition of a few words there, we have now the measure which is submitted to the house. It is one upon which a good deal of work has been done by the 'permanent officials of the department and -I think I can say this without fear of being misunderstood-also no inconsiderable amount of work by the head of the department.
In the act of 1878 there occur these words:
For the more complete examination of the public accounts of the dominion, and for the reporting thereon to the House of Commons, the Governor General may. under the great seal of Canada, appoint an officer, to be called the Auditor General of Canada.
That is the genesis of the law providing for the appointment of the auditor general. We have not had very many auditors general in this country. They have usually held office for a long term of years and they are, or they should be, entirely free from any governmental control. The section in question is maintained in the new revision, but cognizance i3 taken of the magnitude of the public service and the inconsistency of requiring an officer to perform administrative duties while at the same time acting as a judge of the administration's actions.
The auditor general, in practice, must commit himself to the propriety of the expenditures, by applying on behalf of a disbursing department, to the Minister of Finance, for a letter of credit. But as he then loses control over the credit thus established, if payments are improperly made by the departments, his redress is to make an adverse report to the House of Commons. Moreover, as the act now stands, the auditor general may, to all intents and purposes, be excluded from any intimate knowledge of the activities of the Department of Finance.
I confess to the house that I found it, and still find it, somewhat difficult to understand just why the statute was framed in the form in which it is. Of all departments to which in my judgment the auditor general should have the freest access, the Department of Finance is the one. But as it stands, he has less freedom of access to that department than to almost any other department of the public service. The change which we have now recommended relieves the auditor general from any responsibility over the administration of the public revenues and expenditures, but it broadens his audit control, giving him the right to investigate every activity of the public service and particularly those of the Department of Finance, while control of all expenditure commitments is to be vested in a central organization. This central control is to be accomplished by the creation of a new division, headed by an officer to be known as the comptroller of the treasury, appointed by the governor In council but removable from office for misbehaviour. In other words, he holds his office during good conduct.
To give the comptroller directive control, the practice of expenditures by letters of credit will to a great extent disappear. I apprehend that members of former governments are familiar with the practice now prevailing; but I doubt whether most hon. members realize that after the estimates are passed the department applies for a letter of credit and with that letter of credit, authorized by order in council, it enters upon the expenditure of the amounts for which it receives credit. For instance, department A may apply for a letter of credit for $10,000,000. The responsible officer places, with the bank or a bank, his letter of credit and proceeds then, through his own accounting staff, in his own office, as a separate and distinct part of the machinery of government, to deal with and disburse that money. In my judgment, that is not sound administrative finance. Whether or not this measure commends itself to the house, I am not in a position to say,
Revenue and Audit Act

because the house has not yet had an opportunity to consider it in detail. I presume, however, that every hon. member believes that centralised control with respect to the estimates voted by parliament is absolutely essential if we are to maintain that relation between appropriations on the one hand and expenditures on the other. And we have endeavoured to deal with it in that sense.
If you will analyze the bill, you will find that while the practice of granting letters of credit has disappeared, there will be substituted therefor, through the accounting branch, what we believe will be efficient and effective control over all expenditures made on behalf of the Dominion of Canada.
I need hardly say-and I make this statement in no critical sense-that during the years the accounting branches of the several departments have engaged a very large number of employees, men and women. Once you have a letter of credit granted to a department, you have made that department almost an independent branch of government. It keeps its own accountants, bookkeepers and accounting staff, and the only control which this country has over these expenditures is exercised after the expenditures have been made, and through the auditor general's office.
One of the real problems which I, speaking personally, experienced in connection with the accounting system of the country at the moment arose out of the fact that it was almost impossible to ascertain what sums of money we were obligated to pay at a given time. For instance, when the right hon. gentleman came into power he could not, by applying to any officer in the Department of Finance, ascertain what sums of money were due for payment within a particular time. He knew, of course, what the estimates were; he knew what the charges against the consolidated revenues were by statute. But he could not, as one should be able in a business, inquire of a given official, "What do your obligations to-day amount to?" Nor could that official say, "The obligations to-day amount to blank dollars".
Need I point out to this house that in the United States they have from day to day a statement from the treasury. I suppose it is within the memory of most hon. members- they must have seen it in the daily press- that a statement comes from the treasury department indicating the receipts and expenditures and the balance which is maintained upon a basis of very complete accounting, such as cannot develop under the system which we now have in vogue.
There is one other difficulty and it is this. As matters stand to-day, not only was the right

hon. gentleman unable to ascertain the fact to which I have directed attention, but on August 7 it was impossible for his successor to ascertain the exact financial situation so far as obligations and liabilities were concerned. That is to say, he was not able to ascertain just what the position was with respect to the several appropriations mentioned and designated in the estimates. And I take it that the proper system of accounting would be to maintain an appropriation ledger containing a statement of each several appropriation of public moneys and that the payments made from time to time should be charged against that, so that at the end of the day's business if I desired information I might be able without much difficulty, assisted with modern mechanical devices, to ascertain the exact position with respect to our payments out on the appropriation made. That is one of the ends aimed at by this legislation.
The treasury board is an integral part of our government and financial system. I need hardly say to the house that that board is comprised of members of the administration and the deputy minister receives an additional compensation for the duties he discharges as secretary of that board.

Yes, the Deputy Minister of Finance. It has been found at times that when the proper officers sit down, with the members of the government who comprise the treasury board, to prepare the estimates, there is some difficulty in ascertaining the exact obligations which must be met in the incoming year and which have arisen out of the balance of contractual obligations created in the year just passed. Under the system I have mentioned that was inevitable. Frequently we have had supplementary estimates at the close of the fiscal year, or main estimates for the new year which are swollen by expenditures jvhich really belonged to the former year. I gave an illustration of that the other day. I do not mean to reflect in any sense upon the administration of my right hon. friend, but this difficulty has arisen because of a system which is illustrated by the department of the King's Printer. That department is supposed to collect from the other departments from month to month the accounts which have been rendered for printing done, but one knows that when the answer is given that all goes into the same pocket and must come out of the same till, it is not easy to maintain that strict accountability which is the basis, in my judgment, of the maintenance

Revenue and Audit Act
and sound conception of public obligations. This bill provides that no contract may be signed or a commitment entered into unless the comptroller of the treasury certifies that there is an unencumbered balance under the appropriate vote available to defray such charges as will fall due during the fiscal year.

I beg formally to move the amendment which I suggested last week, as follows:
That section 1 of Bill No. 18 be stricken out and the following be substituted therefor:
1. Subsection 4 of section 29 of chapter 22 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
4. In all examinations for entrance into the civil service, the persons named on such special list, who are found to possess the necessary qualifications, shall be named in the order of merit on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates, and all other persons who have been on active service overseas, in the military or naval forces of His Majesty during the late war, and were at the time of their enlistment or at the date of the passing of this act domiciled in Canada, who have left such service with an honourable record, or who have been honourably discharged, or when any persons who have served overseas as aforesaid, have died owing to such service, the widows of such persons, and who, in either case, obtained sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be named in the list of successful candidates next after any candidates who are in the special list mentioned in subsection 2 of this section, and above all other candidates.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERANS RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I regret
that in this case I cannot support either the original bill as introduced by my good friend the hon. member for Bellechasse or the amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec South. Amongst ex-service men in Canada there is no one who has a higher reputation for having rendered wonderful service in their interests than the hon. member who has just moved the amendment. For the last ten years the house has had the benefit of his wide experience, assistance and advice.
I should like, however, to direct the attention of the committee to the exact significance of what is being done. The effect of the amendment just moved is this: it tones

down materially the original clauses of the bill and confines the preference practically to Canadians and to imperials who were domiciled in Canada in 1914. In other words, as I construe the amendment-and my hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong-the only ones who are excluded by it are imperials who may come to Canada after the date of the passing of this bill.
Since 1919 two distinct preferences have been accorded ex-service men in Canada. The first I should like to call a primary preference and the second a secondary preference. The primary preference is to be found in subsection 2 of section 29 of the Civil Service Act. and with the permission of the committee I shall read that subsection:
The commission shall prepare and maintain a special list of persons in receipt of pensions by reason of their services in the war who,
(a)	have from causes attributable to such service lost capacity for physical exertion to an extent which makes them unfit efficiently to pursue the avocations which they were pursuing before the war;
(b)	have not been successfully reestablished in some other avocation; and
(c)	desire to be placed on such list.
I wish to make clear that there is a primary disability preference list both for Canadian and imperial soldiers, and for allied soldiers, provided they come within the terms of section 33 of the act. The secondary preference is contained in section 29, subsection 4. Without in the slightest degree intending so to do, I think my hon. friend conveyed an erroneous impression when he mentioned the Portuguese, Russians and other allies who might compete with former Canadian exservice men. If my hon. friend will turn to section 33 of the Civil Service Act he will find the following:
No person shall, without the authority of the governor in council, be admitted to any examination unless he is a natural born or naturalized British subject, and also has been a resident of Canada for at least three years.
Before one may undergo an examination the primary requisite is that he must be a British subject and must have been in Canada for at least three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
