speechtext: That is the law.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERANS RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Yes,
but under the act the governor in council may authorize the employment of specially qualified technicians. The situation is that no one to-day can receive a preference unless he or she is a British subject. Therefore the danger from the somewhat fantastic list of allies mentioned by my hon. friend is really eliminated, and we come down to the dues-

Civil Service-Returned Soldiers
tion of discrimination against imperial veterans, those belonging to the British empire.
At this point, in an absolutely non-partisan spirit I wish to make one suggestion to the committee. For the last ten years, in fact since 1919, the House of Commons has been very generous indeed in the consideration of the problems of the organized ex-service men of Canada. Year after year we have had committee after committee appointed. There was a royal commission to investigate the problems of civil reestablishment, and in every single instance so far as my memory serves me and if I am wrong some hon. member will undoubtedly correct me the organized ex-service men of Canada have been consulted in regard to any proposed change in veterans' legislation. Last year, under the excellent leadership of my hon. friend from Quebec South, we had in the work of the committee and in its report to the house one of the most inspiring incidents in Canadian parliamentary history: the splendid report of the committee was adopted unanimously by parliament. To-day in Canada we have the Canadian Legion representing practically all the organized ex-service men in the country. So far as my knowledge goes, that organization has not been consulted regarding the amendment now before us. For ten years we have given a preference to imperial soldiers, and the only possible effect of the amendment of the hon. member for Quebec South would be to eliminate those who come to Canada after the passing of this act. The number of these men is being reduced year after year. The Canadian Legion and other organized ex-service bodies are prepared to discuss this matter and to send recommendations to parliament as they have in years gone by. Next August or September in the city of Toronto the annual convention of the Canadian Legion will be held and will deal with this very point. The biennial conference of the British Empire Service League representing ex-service men throughout the whole empire is to meet in Toronto in a month or two to discuss problems affecting the ex-service men throughout the British Empire. In view of all these considerations my suggestion to the mover of the amendment and the sponsor of the bill is that we might very well postpone consideration of the matter for at least a year, or until we have ' concrete and comprehensive recommendations from the ex-service men of Canada in convention assembled.
If the matter were urgent I should be pleased to deal with it immediately. I do not
believe a single member of the committee has received a specific complaint in regard to the present preference. At the last biennial conference of the British Empire Service League held in Canada in the year 1925 that great leader of the British army, Sir Douglas Haig, was in attendance. This year we will have with us the great leader of the British navy during the war, Earl Jellicoe, now leader of the British Empire Service League. It would be most unfortunate and at best a futile gesture if at this stage, and in view of the forthcoming conference of empire service men, parliament were to eliminate the preference which for the last ten years Canada has shown. Almost seventeen years have elapsed since the outbreak of hostilities, and any hon. member of this house-and there are many of them-who visit weekly the meetings of ex-service men throughout Canada must recognize the fact that the war veterans are now more or less old men. Those who are qualified by strength and physical capacity to compete in civil service examinations are year by year getting fewer in number.	[DOT]
I appeal most sincerely to the committee to recognize that in days gone by we have had the benefit of expressions of opinion of the Canadian ex-service men regarding these matters. They are a body whose views are of great value and assistance to any government, no matter what government it may be. The desire of ex-service leagues is to do the best they can for ex-service men. I am sure no injury will be done if we lay this matter over until next year when we may have before us the considered recommendations of the exservice men, and we will not be in the position of altering our considered policy on the eve of the convening of the biennial conference of the British Empire Service League.

speechtext:
To prevent any misunderstanding, Mr. Chairman, as to just what this amendment purports to do, perhaps I had better review the bill and the amendment itself. The bill in section 1 proposes to amend section 29 of the Civil Service Act, which is chapter 22 of the revised statutes of Canada. It is proposed to add subsection (5), which to a considerable extent would do away with the returned solders' preference. I understand that the returned soldiers generally throughout the country and the Canadian Legion were opposed to this bill on account of the section which my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) intended to add. An agitation- sprang up and various commands of the legion made requests to members of this house and to others to oppose the bill. Then on May 19 I said that if the bill reached committee I would propose a certain amendment-the amendment which is now before the committee. The amendment does not seek to do away with subsection 2 of section 29, which my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) read, and which gives a particular preference to those who have been injured and are unable to pursue their former vocation and to those who have not been successfully reestablished. The amendment does not propose to touch those men at all. It does not propose to touch section 33, which states that only British subjects may enter the civil service of Canada. But it does propose to amend subsection 4 of section 29. Subsection 4 was originally inserted in the Civil Service Act in 1919. By it the people of Canada gave a preference in the civil service appointments: first, to Canadian soldiers; second, to soldiers who had served in the army or navy of His Majesty; third, to soldiers who had served in the allied forces. I propose by my amendment to take away that preference from those who served in the allied forces. I also propose that the preference which has been given to imperial soldiers shall cease as to any who come here after this date.
There does not seem to be anything in that section which would wreck the British constitution or call for a consultation with anybody in the dominion. The thing is perfectly plain. If the house desires to vote against that principle there is no necessity to go out-

Civil Service-Returned Soldiers
side and consult anybody about it. Since when have we in this house set u,p outside the confines of parliament a kind of soldiers' soviet which must be consulted when we wish to pass legislation? As a matter of fact when pension legislation was brought before this house representatives of the returned soldiers' organizations came before committees which dealt with that legislation. They were treated courteously and their representations were listened to; sometimes they were accepted, sometimes not. But it is an altogether new theory in our parliamentary practice that before we pass any legislation which might directly or indirectly affect certain soldiers, and as I have already explained, will not affect Canadian soldiers and will not affect any imperial soldiers who are now domiciled in Canada,-that forsooth we should wait until the members of the Canadian Legion meet Earl Jellicoe and their imperial comrades in August and decide whether or not we, the parliament of Canada, shall continue to give a preference to people who are now living in England. It seems to me that the case is perfectly plain. It is a matter of indifference to me whether or not this amendment passes, but I wish to make perfectly clear the purport of the amendment, and to show that there is no intention whatsoever of offending any particular class of people Who served in the late war, or of taking away from them any rights which they may have. Those who are British subjects and who served in the army of the empire will prej 'serve their preference provided they are domiciled in Canada now. Those who served in the allied forces will be affected. I know my hon. friend said that the amendment Would not affect ex-service men of the nations which I mentioned, but there is nothing to prevent a Czechoslovakian, a Russian, a Frenchman, a Greek, or a Chinese, or a Japanese, provided they have been naturalized, from taking advantage of this preference, and I do not think it is the view of this house, nor is it the view of the people of Canada, that we should be any more generous to the people of any other nation, particularly at the expense of our own citizens.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERANS RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I fully realize, Mr. Chairman, that it is always a delicate matter to deal with questions in which returned soldiers are involved, but at the same time I think it is the duty of every hon. member to state his position very clearly in a matter of this kind. I have no hesitation in saying that I endorse very fully the stand taken by the hon. member for Quebec South, and also his amendment. In saying this I am not only expressing my opinion as a member of the house but I am drawing on my experience as Secretary of State, under whose supervision comes the work of the Civil Service Commission.
There are two points I wish to make very briefly in connection with this bill and amendment. In the first place, let us not forget that the principle at the basis of the Civil Sendee Act is merit. The act states that candidates to the civil service shall be appointed on merit; there is to be no political or family influence of any kind to interfere with the merits of the respective candidates. An exception was made in favour of returned soldiers, whether imperial or Canadian, as my hon. friend has said. We must not lose sight of the fact that this exception is not in conformity with the principle at the basis of the Civil Sendee Act. Very often, in Montreal and elsewhere, I have seen young men who were candidates at examinations for the civil service; these young men were fully qualified and possessed the necessary merit to be appointed, yet they would see candidates, returned soldiers who were perhaps 35 or 40 points below their marks, appointed in their places. I realize that this may have been a good after-war measure, but the first point I wish to make is that no matter how worthy that principle may be it comes in direct conflict with the very foundation of the Civil Service Act, which is that merit shall prevail over every other consideration.
It therefore follows-and this is my second point-that while we may all desire to give that preference to returned soldiers when it is warrantable, we should not extend the field of preference but should rather try to restrict it as much as is commensurate with those other principles of preference which already exist in favour of soldiers. We have dealt with our returned men; we have enacted pension and other legislation in their favour. Will any hon. gentleman in this house tell me any field other than the civil service in which there is legislation in favour of imperial men, or men from Australia or New Zealand or any other portion of the empire, or even from the other allied forces? If it is all right to give a preference to a returned man of the imperial army who is not domiciled to-day in Canada, why not vote a pension for him? Why not make available to him the other advantages we have granted the returned soldiers in Canada? The time has come when that preference, which is in direct opposition to the principle of merit, the basis of our Civil Service Act, should be firmly restricted to Canadian soldiers already domiciled in
Civil Service-Returned Soldiers

Canada, and to no others. We do not vote pensions for imperial soldiers or Australian soldiers, so I maintain we should no longer give a preference in civil service appointments to soldiers other than those who strictly belong to Canada. We do not send our men overseas to enjoy a preference in English civil service appointments; we do not send them to other parts of the empire. Last year, or two years ago, the House of Commons agreed to that modified application of the principle of preference in connection with the bill having to do with the Department of National Revenue. There are certain classes of employees under the Minister of National Revenue, who are appointed by him, and a provision similar to the amendment of my hon. friend from Quebec South was adopted. In other words, it was decided that preference should be given only to Canadian soldiers domiciled in Canada.
'-No very serious inconvenience may be caused by waiting another year, but I do submit that we meet to achieve results. This matter has been before the house for many years; year after year the bill has been moved, but no results have been obtained. I believe the amendment of the hon member for Quebec South is quite in conformity with the conditions as we find them to-day, and as far as I am concerned I shall not only support his amendment but shall also recommend very strongly to the committee that we deal with this matter at once and limit the preference to soldiers who are domiciled in Canada. I think that will meet with general approval.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover of this bill amending the Civil Service Act which grants a preference to veterans. I think that it is the proper time to enact such a bill. Ever since the Conservative party is in power, we have heard on many occasions the cry of "Canada First". Since the Conservatives favour the policy of "Canada First", they should appoint "Canada First" men to positions in the civil service.
I have no objection however, to the amendment of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). To grant a preference to Canadian veterans residing in Canada, means simply doing justice to the patriotism they displayed in the Great war. On the other hand, in giving this preference, care should be taken that public affairs will not suffer from the appointment of persons who might prove incompetent. As the present government prides itself in giving the country an exemplary administration, it should discriminate in the choice of its employees. This preference should only be granted to those who are capable of rending efficient service.
I am in favour of the amendment which purports to grant a preference to Canadian veterans domiciled in Canada. I fail to see why we should grant this preference to veterans of other countries or those of other British nations. We should keep our civil service positions for Canadians residing in Canada.
Again I wish to congratulate the mover of this bill. He is inspired by a truly Canadian spirit, he is patriotic and, perhaps, more sincere than this government.
Mr. LaVERGNE: I have been led to believe in Canada first, especially during and since the last campaign, and to-night I still hold to that principle-Canada and Canadians first. I must say that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Quebec South is most generous. I know of no legislation similar to this in England, South Africa, Australia or New Zealand. I may be wrong many times, but I certainly do believe in being loyal to one's principles; and if we are true to our principles we must first stand by our own nationals. In my opinion, it is false sentiment to speak about the empire or things imperial in relation to this bill. Someone

Civil Service-Returned Soldiers
must begin somewhere, and as I say, I know of no other dominion that has passed legislation such as is proposed here. So far as I am concerned, I will vote for the amendment, because half a loaf is better than no bread. But I should prefer to have the bill as it was. I believe in Canada first.

speechtext:
I am sorry I cannot
agree to the postponement of this bill until next session. The matter has already been before this house on two occasions. It was introduced last year and owing to the necessity for closing the house in rather a hurry it was not passed. But I presented it again this year at the beginning of the session. It has been before hon. members for a considerable time and anyone who wanted to study it has had ample opportunity to do so. Moreover, the principle is not new. As the hon. member for St. James pointed out a moment ago, the very principle embodied in this bill was adopted unanimously by the house in 1928, when the revision of the National Revenue Act was before the house. The amendment was moved by my hon. friend from Quebec South. He proposed that the veterans' preference be restricted to Canadian veterans and his amendment was adopted on May 16, 1928. If hon. members wish to refer to Hansard they will find the report in volume 3 of 1928, at page 3064. They will see that the amendment restricting the veterans' preference to Canadian veterans was moved by my hon. friend and was adopted unanimously. That was more than two years ago. This principle was embodied in the bill presented last year and the same bill was presented again at the beginning of this session. I do not see, therefore, any necessity for postponing the matter another year for the purpose of giving the house time to study the principle of the bill, because it is a principle with which the house is perfectly familiar-a principle which, as I have shown, was adopted by the house more than two years ago.
Let me say a word to my hon. friends who are fearful of the bill because, as they suggest, it is the thin edge of the wedge towards abolition of the veterans' preference. I would point out to them that the bill is the best means we could possibly have of retaining the veterans' preference. If they wish to retain that preference in favour of Canadian soldiers, I ask them to vote for the bill; because once it is known throughout the country that we grant, in our civil service appointments, a preference not only to our own soldiers but also the soldiers of all the allied armies which took part in the war, there will be such an outcry against the 22110-187
veterans' preference that strong demand will be made for its abolition. The result will be that the whole preference will go by the board-not only the preference in favour of imperial soldiers, the preference in favour of the soldiers of South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, and other dominions, but also the preference in favour of our own Canadian Veterans. I say to my hon. friends, therefore, that if they want to retain the preference to Canadian soldiers they must be sensible about it and restrict it to our own veterans, citizens actually domiciled in Canada.
There is no allied country that has been so generous as we have been. Neither South Africa, New Zealand, India, nor any other part of the empire has given us any preference in its civil service. Try to get a job in the civil service in England, or in South Africa or Australia. Say to the authorities there, "I fought for you during the Great war. I came to your rescue." They will say, "That was very nice of you and we thank you very much. But we have to look after our own citizens first in appointments to our civil service." What others do for themselves I do not see why we should not do for ourselves.
There have been great abuses of the preference in favour of imperial soldiers. I cited some facts when I presented the bill for second reading. We have imported from England at least twenty prison guards. We brought them in directly from England and gave them jobs in our penitentiaries in preference to our own Canadian citizens-men who had been living here all their lives, paying taxes and contributing their efforts to the advancement of the country. We imported these prison guards and gave them jobs in our penitentiaries when Canadian soldiers could have done the work as well. We import other classes also into the civil service, engineers, surveyors, map draftsmen, and so on. I obtained a list at the last session on a return, and if hon. members are desirous of seeing it I can supply them with copies. They would be edified to see how many, I will not say foreigners, but non-Canadians, have entered the civil service without complying in the least with the requirements of the Civil Service Act.
It seems to me that in times like this, when there are so many people out of work looking for jobs, to earn their daily bread for themselves and their families, we should at least

that this is not the time to bring in legislation of this kind. On previous occasions these soldier bodies have come back to the committee and asked that we reverse our ruling and go back to the previous practice. They admitted their mistake and I think in the future we would be doing well, not only by the soldiers but by ourselves, if we carried out our own ideas.
These men are fast passing away; they are dying at the rate of about 150 or 200 per year. I was staggered a few weeks ago when I Was told that there were not 150,000 men living to-day who had seen service in France. Those who remain are year after year becoming more disabled and crippled because of the infirmities suffered in service and I do not think in their last hours, in their last days or their last years we should pass legislation which will make them think we are growing careless of their interests and that this is the thin edge of the wedge which will ultimately deprive them of all preference which they have enjoyed in the past. If there were any ills time is rapidly curing them, and all this parliament and country has to do is simply nothing; these ills, if they are such, will be righted. For the life of me I cannot see just what this amendment is going to accomplish. The number concerned will constantly decrease until but few possible applicants remain, and, as I said before, I do not think it is worth the time of this house to consider the matter. I concur heartily in the sentiments of the hon. member who introduced this amendment, and I have done so in the past, but I do not think that this is the time to introduce an amendment of this kind.

If no other hon. member desires to speak, I should like to make this observation. My right hon. friend is entirely in error with respect to the Welland canal transaction. He will, I suppose, insist until the crack of doom that he is right, just as he does with respect to no part of the war cost having been paid out of current revenues. The Minister oi Finance at that time conclusively proved that there were expenditures for the war period that were paid out of current taxation. Nevertheless, the right hon. gentleman declines to be convinced.
In this instance the fact is that there was a contract extended by the right hon. gentleman's government for the construction of a section of the Welland canal, and the sum of $7,000,000 was voted for the purpose of meeting the claims of the contractors under their several contracts for the fiscal year ending the 31st March, 1931. The contract contained a provision whereby the contractors were to finish their work by a given date and it was also provided in the contract itself that if they went forward and finished their work within the term of the contract, they of course could not be paid during that fiscal year any moneys further than were appropriated by parliament. In this particular instance the contractors expanded their effort and earned $2,000,000 within the time limit of their contracts and the notices called for by the contracts were given, pointing out that they could not receive their pay until parliament had voted the money either in supplementary estimates or in regular estimates in the subsequent year. That is what happened; the contract provided for it and the men were paid accordingly. I know, of course, how hopeless it is to endeavour to induce my right hon. friend, having taken the position he has, to admit that these facts bring the matter entirely without the case which I was endeavouring to make this afternoon. Had the analogy been complete as contended for by the right hon. gentleman, it would have been a case in which the government that succeeded his, provided by a contract for an expenditure of additional sums of money. That, as I have

said, was not the case. All that happened was that the contractors, strictly within the letter of the contract, by endeavouring to complete it within the term fixed therein, thereby earned additional money which, under the terms of the contract itself, could not be paid until it was voted by parliament. I make that statement merely because I cannot think the right hon. gentleman desires to leave an erroneous impression. Yet the facts are there so that he who runs may read, and a wayfaring child need not err therein. We can put it as strongly as that. The "wayfaring" is good.
With respect to the second matter, namely, unemployment relief, we have threshed that out so much I am not going to refer to it further than to say that we lived up absolutely to the obligations imposed upon the government by parliament and laid before the house, within the time limit set by the statute, a report of the moneys that had been appropriated and expended. I was very careful to point out last year that inasmuch as appropriations would be made that might not be wholly expended, it must clearly be meant that they be made out of the $20,000,000 itself.
I am grateful to the right hon. gentleman for his general acceptance of the principles of the proposed measure, and I assure him that if it becomes law it is quite clear that neither this nor any other executive will be able to get a cheque past the Comptroller General under the circumstances to which he alludes, for the simple and obvious reason that unless there is a credit to the appropriate item, the cheque will not issue. That is the whole purpose of the measure. It binds alike the government and the officials of the various departments.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the select standing committee on banking and commerce.

The reason for section 3 is to provide for the winding up of existing business, and for those who are entitled to superannuation. When the mint was established a working arrangement was made with respect to those matters. 'If the bill now before us is passed it will become law when all these matters have been disposed of. Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Minister of Marine) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize a loan to the New Westminster harbour commissioners not exceeding $300,000, to complete the grain elevator structure and facilities on the south side of New Westminster harbour and provide for payment of outstanding indebtedness chargeable thereto or arising therefrom, upon approval by the governor in council of detailed plans, specifications and estimates for such works and the deposit of debentures of the corporation to cover such loan; and the loan available to the corporation shall be for the amount of expenditure certified by an officer of the Department of Marine who shall have supervision and control of all expenditures.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacDonald (South Cape Breton) in the chair.
Be fere this resolution is adopted I should like to ask the Minister of Marine one or two questions. How is it proposed to pay 'back this money, or have any arrangements been made for paying it back?

It will be paid back
out of dues, the same as any other harbour commission.

Is it a fact that the minister
purposes to put on harbour dues in the port of New Westminster?

I think so; I think
it is the intention to do that.

I am not going to object to
the lending of $300 000 to complete the grain elevator, but I must register a vigorous protest if any dues are put on in connection with the harbour at New Westminster.
I should like to refer to one or two objections concerning the placing of dues. The Fraser river has always been clear of dues and this has been largely the means of building up the port of New Westminster. We have come to the point of development where a great many of us believe that if dues are imposed the river shipping will be affected and turned away from that port probably to ports to the south of us. I should like to point out to the minister the position in which the city of New Westminster would find itself if through the imposition of dues shipping was affected. In 1911 there was little deep sea shipping through the port of New Westminster. At that time preparations were being
New Westminster Harbour

made for the use of the Panama canal. On the completion of the Panama canal the city of New Westminster spent considerable money on its docks, in anticipation of shipping activities. It was not until after the war that the Panama canal began to be effective as a route for shipping, and from that time shipping began to increase on the Fraser river. For that reason the port flourished and a few years ago the city guaranteed the interest on $300,000 in connection with cold storage facilities and also gave a fixed assessment of $5,000 on property worth over $2,000,000, That assessment was guaranteed for a period of ten years. In addition the city agreed to take $30,000 worth of space in the cold storage plant. At the present time the city of New Westminster has not been called upon to pay any of that guarantee. But I have it on good authority from the owners of vessels who are using the port and the cold storage facilities that the imposition of dues would have a very serious effect. The fact that New Westminster has been a free port has always made it attractive to ship owners. Now it is proposed to impose dues to cover up some of the blunders that have been made in connection with the building of the elevator. We all asked for an elevator, but we are not responsible for the mistakes made by those who had charge of its location and construction, and it is very unfair that the port should be penalized on this account. I certainly'register a very strong protest against the imposition of dues. The trade of our port has been growing year by year until for the past fiscal year we had large ocean going vessels call almost every day, due mainly to the fact that the port is free. Let me read a resolution passed by the city council of New Westminster on March 12, 1931, a copy of which was sent to the hon. minister. It is in these words:
Press despatches state the chairman of the Westminster harbour board has filed application with you for permission to increase present rate of harbour dues on this port. As you are aware the city of New Westminster has recently achieved importance as a deep sea port due altogether to the activities of the Pacific Coast Terminals Limited in which the city of New Westminster is heavily involved financially in addition to the city's own investment of half a million dollars in dock construction all within city limits. The Westminster harbour board has had no part in nor rendered any practical assistance in this port development work at the city of New Westminster where over ninety per cent of all port business originates and arrives. The construction of an elevator by the harbour board across the river in south Westminster in an isolated location away from all the traffic movement of the port and at a cost of eight hundred thousand dollars was an experimental undertaking by the 
harbour board entirely divorced from the port a('t.ivitics of the city of New Westminster and while we have no objection to the imposition ot whatever charges appear necessary and proper m traffic moving over the elevator facilities we respectfully but strenuously protest against surcharges imposed on port traffic developed by this city and its complemental organization the Pacific Coast Terminals Limited to support the experiment carried out by the harbour board without the consent or approval of the citizens of New Westminster. Additional dues would be to handicap traffic in using port facilities without any resulting benefit to the city.
That resolution indicates the feeling of practically all the citizens not only of New Westminster but of the surrounding municipalities against the imposition of dues, for this port has been free from its inception, and to make the proposed change would mean driving away much of our shipping to other ports. We claim that the port of New Westminster should not be penalized on account of the blunders made during the construction of the elevator.

Mr. Chairman, whether or not dues will be imposed rests with the harbour commissioners of New Westminster. Of course, we have control over the commission, but we do not want to exercise that control too rigidly. As the hon. member says, the elevator was an extravagant experiment made 'by the commission. .
Yes.

Well, this government had nothing to do with that undertaking, for it was initiated in 1928 under the former government and the structure was completed in April, 1930-before we came into power. The hon. gentleman is right as to the cost of the elevator being over $800,000; to be exact, it cost $821,000. The commission sold $700,000 of debentures at 95 and a fraction, on which they realized $671,000. Now, as the hon. member knows, the elevator started to sink into the river, and no one will rent space in such an unstable structure. The commission contend that if repairs were made to the foundations to the extent of $50,000 or' $60,000 they would be able to rent all the available space, and it is said the rental would provide sufficient revenue to pay interest on the loan.
I do not know. To-day we are faced with this situation. The commission owe certain moneys which they cannot repay unless they borrow from the government; and they must repair the foundations, otherwise the elevator will be of no use. Under the circumstances I think it is a matter of urgency that the government should lend the commissioners the $300,000, provided the money is well spent- and the elevators put into good order.

New Westminster Harbour

I am not objecting to the

maintopic: SUPPLY-PACIFIC FISHERMEN PISHING CONDITIONS ON BRITISH COLUMBIA COAST -STATEMENT BY MB. HANSON (SKEENA)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the house a very important question which I think should be considered by the government. I refer to the condition of the fishermen on the Pacific coast, extending from Washington to Alaska. I have a resolution before me which was unanimously adopted at a mass meeting held in Prince Rupert, and which has received several endorsations from public bodies, which I am not going to take time to read. However, I desire to place on Hansard the resolution:
. a mass meeting held in the Moose Hall ln 1 rmce Rupert, B.C., on June 12th, the fmmwmg resolution was unanimously adopted: Whereas the prices of halibut and salmon presently obtained are not proportional (or below any proportion) to the cost of fishing operations, and
Whereas the principal market for Canadian halibut and salmon is in the United States which is protected by two cents duty against Canadian halibut and salmon, and \\ hereas the Canadian fish buyers have already declared that they cannot pay any higher prices for halibut and salmon than those prevailing now,

Be it resolved that a subsidy of two cents per pound is the minimum assistance necessary tor Canadian halibut and salmon industries to carry on and to prevent any further aggravation ot already disastrous business depression, and
Be it further resolved that copies of this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, Minister of Fisheries, Olof Hanson, M.P., A. W. Neill, M.P. and local public bodies for endorsation and action.
The situation outlined here is endorsed by such public bodies as the board of trade, and I have a good many telegrams which I will' not attempt to read.
This is something that the government should take very seriously into consideration. The production of salmon and halibut on the Pacific coast, we know, exceeds the consumption in Canada. Our Canadian fleet have developed a very good business and they are looking for a market; and their only market for halibut is the United States. The United States has imposed a duty of 2 cents per pound on fish going into that country, and in addition to this handicap which our fishermen have to face, this government has raised a tariff against everything which the fishing industry requires in order to carry on its business. Our fishermen must have gasoline, hooks, rubber boots, special clothing and so on, and naturally a duty against these articles must operate to their disadvantage. They are receiving 2 cents less for their fish and they have to pay about twice as much as their competitors for the necessary equipment to enable them to catch their fish. The Canadian government has seen fit to extend some assistance to the farmers of western Canada, but no consideration has been given to the fishing industry. I submit that the government should do something to keep the Canadian fishing fleet alive. It does not seem right that, besides receiving less for their fish, they should be expected to pay more for their equipment.
Prince Rupert is the logical point geographically through which to ship to the market fish caught in the North Pacific waters, and it derives a certain benefit from the fact that the fleet come into that port. And as the terminus of the Canadian National railway is at Prince Rupert, it is a great source of revenue to the Canadian National Railways to have the American fleet land their fish there for transportation to the markets. The handicap under which our Canadian fleet is working is one with which I am quite familiar, and it is a serious problem. The question is whether or not the government should take steps to prevent the American fleet from landing their catches at the port of Prince

Pacific Fishermen-Mr. Neill
Rupert. But that would mean a considerable loss to the merchants of that city as well as to the Canadian National Railways. Prince Rupert depends upon the fishing fleet, however, and it seems to me that every loyal Canadian should stand behind our own fishing fleet as much as possible. I would therefore suggest to the government that they make some adjustment in the present situation with a view to putting our Canadian fishing fleet on the same basis as the American fleet. I am not here to criticize or to say how this should be done, but I should think that negotiations with the United States government in an effort to abolish the 2 cents per pound duty on Canadian fish would probably help to solve the problem.
Just to illustrate the difficulties our Canadian fishermen have to face in competition with our neighbours to the south of us, I might mention one item-gasoline. At the present time the price in Prince Rupert, for the same quantity of gas, is 88 cents as against 25 to 30 cents in Seattle. This item alone .will give the house an idea of the impossibility of competing with the American fleet, especially when we remember, as I have already pointed out,'that the Canadian fishermen get 2 cents less for their fish. There are hon. members on both sides of the house who have the same information that I have in regard to this subject, and I am sure they will assist me in my efforts to have the present situation improved. The resolution passed by the fishermen's association will show how urgent it is that something should be done, and done shortly.
I wish to quote briefly from a report that appeared in the Vancouver Sun:
Prince Rupert Mob Bars U.S. Fishboat
Prince Rupert, May 18.-The American halibut boat Estep, laden with a catch of halibut, was last night denied the right of tying up alongside a dock in Prince Rupert with a view to selling her fish on the local exchange this morning.
As the vessel came alongside, it is stated, she was met by a mob of fifteen or sixteen men who warned the skipper not to tie up or else his lines would be cut.
This is a serious situation. I am not a bolshevik and I certainly do not believe in revolution, but I submit that in the face of a situation such as this it is imperative that something should be done. Our fishermen should be allowed to earn a few dollars in the fishing season to enable them to live during the coming winter. Otherwise they will become a charge on the government. I have done my best to explain the situation, to show how very serious it is, and I trust that the government will give the matter very careful attention.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PACIFIC FISHERMEN PISHING CONDITIONS ON BRITISH COLUMBIA COAST -STATEMENT BY MB. HANSON (SKEENA)
speechtext:
The situation outlined by the last speaker is one that must command the sympathy of everyone who is at all familiar with it. It comes home particularly to me, not only because I know the district, but because, if you sub stitute the word salmon for the word halibut, the situation as indicated by the hon. member for Skeena is entirely reproduced in the district I represent. The hon. member referred to a meeting at which the resolution was passed. This was not any hole and corner meeting passing resolutions in the dark; it. was a large meeting reported in the newspapers. Among other things they decided that all their halibut boats as they came from the banks-they go out on eight or ten day trips-would have to be tied up, because it does not pay them to go out at the price of gas, and with the price they receive for their . fish. A number of the boats had been already tied up, it was stated, and the rest would be tied up too. The Alaskan fishermen were agreeable to the proposal that fishing should cease for a ten day period between trips to keep down the production of fish, but the boats operating from Seattle were opposed to that. There is a genuine and rather bitter feeling among the fishermen and it is very widespread. The hon. member referred to the American fishing fleet, and the suggestion of violence if they tied up. There is no doubt about it that the situation at the present time is acute. We have no market for our halibut in Canada. It all goes to the United States, and the catch centres around Prince Rupert. A large number of American fishermen find it to their profit to ship halibut into the United States in bond through Prince Rupert, and the Prince Rupert people derive great benefit therefrom. They supply boxes, the labour of salting and cleaning, and so forth. And a much smaller number of Canadian fishermen do the same thing. The trouble is that there is a duty of two cents per pound on Canadian fish going into the United States and the result is that the American fisherman ships his fish through in bond and does not have to pay the two cents duty while the Canadian fisherman coming along to his own home port receives two cents per pound less than his American competitor, an alien and foreigner. In years gone by it was not such a bitter thing because the price was up around 15, 16 and 18 cents per pound, but now when it is down to five, six and eight cents per pound, two cents per pound makes the difference between a loss and the ability to operate.
Naturally, as men will, they turned to the nearest and most obvious remedy, and they have asked by this resolution that the govern-
Pacific Fishermen-Mr. Neill

ment bonus them to the extent of two cents per pound in order to put them on a par with the American fisherman. It is quite natural that they should take that point of view, but we with a larger knowledge of international relations and law must consider whether it would be wholly wise or have the beneficial effect which we as well as they desire. I have before me the American tariff. The item which refers to this matter is number 303, and its effect is that if any country importing goods into the United States in any way .bonuses the producer or manufacturer of those articles, then in such case in addition to the duties otherwise imposed by the act, a sum equivalent to the net amount of such bounty or grant shall be added to the duty. The result would be that if we gave our men a bonus of two cents per pound, automatically they would have to pay four cents per pound on fish going into the United States. That would be the automatic result and would not require any process of law. In that case, our men would be no better off than before.
There is another method the adoption of which might put our men on a par, and that is the imposition of a port tax on American fishermen bringing their fish into Prince Rupert. That would not be considered to be in the nature of a bonus, and would put the fishermen on a level. However, that suggests another danger: the American fishermen might put on a fast carrier to ship their fish direct to Seattle. The ultimate and only market is in the United States; there is no market in Canada. In that case the town of Prince Rupert would be a heavy loser because it would lose all the trade derived iby the handling of this large American supply. Speaking roughly, out of 30,000,000 pounds caught in a given period, 22,000,000 pounds would be American caught and the balance Canadian. Such action would hit the town of Prince Rupert very heavily.
It has been contemplated by the Department of Fisheries for many years to take such action in the hope that the American fishermen, who would be deprived of a livelihood, would use their influence with the politicians at Washington to get the two-cent duty on fish going into the States taken off. That would be a highly desirable thing and is really what our men want. Unfortunately we cannot compel the Americans to change their tariff. Another factor to be considered is the wholesale fishing interests centred around Seattle. They are much more powerful and have greater influence than the fishermen scattered up and down the coast. For years they have been trying to bring pressure to bear on Washington to have the fish going 
through Prince Rupert stopped altogether, and I am afraid that any suggestion of this port tax might be the last straw which would enable them to use their influence in order to have all fish stopped from going through Prince Rupert. All these things must 'be considered before any action is taken. In the meantime, I think it would be much better if we made friendly representations to the United States. We have a capable ambassador there and this matter might be taken up in a friendly way. Adjustments might be made, such as the granting of a small item in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway, or other matter and a beneficial result might be obtained.
I have been referring to the condition of the halibut men, which condition is paralleled by that of the trollers to the south, who handtroll for salmon. I speak now more particularly of the west coast of Vancouver island. American trollers come up from Seattle and troll the banks which are just outside our territorial waters. They meet our men who have come out from Vancouver island and they fish on a common basis. Very often the American boats run into our harbours at night and then go out in the morning, which process is continued until their boats are filled, when they go to Seattle where there is the only market for spring salmon. Our men receive two cents per pound less for their fish than do the Americans and, as I said before, two cents per pound on a price of four, five and six cents per pound is a great deal. The American has another advantage, he is able to obtain his gasoline much cheaper, and gasoline makes up 35 per cent of the cost of operating these boats. He obtains his gasoline for less than half of the price paid by the Canadian fisherman. That is reason enough for the government doing away with the tax which they placed last September on gasoline. I remember the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) pleading along with myself that the government should not impose a tax. At that time there was no tax on the class of gasoline used by these men, but one was put on despite our efforts. There was a duty imposed of 2} cents per gallon and we were told the legend that the price would not go up in spite of the tariff being raised. That beautiful fantasy has now passed into the realm of the classics; it has gone back into the same class as the oriental metaphor we read about in the description of battles by the biblical historian. He would say that the Israelites or the Philistines were in number as the sands of the sea when perhaps the total strength would not exceed

Pacific Fishermen-Mr. Neill
50,000 or 100,000 fighting men. That is the same sort of beautiful imagery which obtains when we are told that the tariff will not increase the price. However, it has gone by the board.
If the price were raised only 2i cents per gallon it might not be very milch, but the Customs Act contains a provision which increases this difference in price. I have not the time at my disposal to read the whole provision, but its effect is that if they do not get you under one item they will get you under another. The provision states that in no case shall the value for duty be less than the actual cost of production at the place of shipment plus profit, etc., We say to the United States:	You do not know your own
business, you do not know the price of your own gasoline; we will settle what the price is and what profit you shall make. Our men are barred from going over to Seattle and buying gasoline at six cents per United States gallon, which is equal to 7'2 cents per imperial gallon. The customs men were told that that was the price at which it was selling all over the United States, but they replied: They do not know their own business, there is a rate war on. How do we know there is a rate war on? That price is universal from one side of the country to the other. Do they not know their own business? We might as well go to some foreign nation and interfere with their tariff. The government said, "There is a rate war on and we will not believe the evidence before our eyes, that thousands of gallons are being sold every day at that price." I read the other day in the newspapers that Brazil had put a tax of 10 shillings per sack on coffee, and either the whole or a part of that 10 shilling tax was to be devoted to buying coffee and taking it out to sea to dump it in order to keep up the price of the coffee remaining. Why do not we go down there and interfere with that practice, and say: That is not the way to do things?
As a result of our monkeying with the tariff, by way of dumping duty there is a duty to-day of 8.5 cents per gallon. When our men run into Seattle with their fish the logical thing is to bring gasoline back, but the present duty- duty alone-on gasoline is about 10 per cent higher than the total price to the American consumer. The duty is 8.5 cents per gallon, and we have to pay that in addition to the price. The American is able to purchase it at 7.2 cents per gallon, which make a nice situation. That does not sound much like "Canada first". Our fisherman is paying 10 per cent more in duty than the United States
fisherman pays altogether and yet the latter competes with us in the same water and receives two cents per pound more for his fish. Is it any wonder that these men about whom my hon. friend from Skeena speaks are getting ugly? As I said before, the cost of gas is about 35 per cent of the cost of operating these boats. To put it roughly, it will mean, instead of paying 35 cents on the dollar for gas, they will have to pay 75 cents. Hon. members can appreciate that when the price of fish has fallen as it has. I am advised by recent letters that the United States, I think it is the local state government, is proposing to help their own fisherman out; they are going to relieve him of a 5 cents state tax which they imposed. I had better not tell the government this or they will be wanting to impose another duty of 5 per cent. It appears to me that we are insisting on the United States raising their own tariff.
I want to give one or two quotations indicative of the situation to show that I am not exaggerating the case in any way. It does not matter to the house whom these letters come from, but I am prepared to give the names if necessary. This is from one letter I have received:
Our fish prices on the grounds now is as low as 5 cents per pound dressed, head on; fishermen paying 24 cents per gallon for gas cannot even hope to make a living out of the trolling so we must get some relief on our gasoline.
Another man says:
The United States government is assisting their fishermen over these hard times, while our government is trying to cripple our fishing industry. The fish prices this year are less than half of last year's prices, while gas prices are only 2 cents less than last year's prices at the oil stations here. The trollers here have made nothing and a number of fishermen have no gas to go out fishing with. God only knows what is going to happen, one sure thing the government will have to keep them and their families this coming winter. I would ask you in the name of the fishermen to use all your power in getting this dumping duty taken off gasoline.
I might say that every one of these is from a representative of some association of fishermen and not from an individual. This is another letter:
This gas dumping duty is working a hardship on the fishing industry of British Columbia, and instead of helping conditions is just doing the reverse. If the government does not take this matter in hand and give the industry a chance to stabilize itself they will have all these trollers on the bread line next winter. Why cannot the government put gas on the free list for commercial fishing purposes and make the oil combines in Canada come down to reason; there is no reason whatsoever why we should have to pay 24 cents a gallon for gas in British Columbia-

speechtext:
The tariff imposed last September. There is nothing in the present budget about gasoline. The letter I was quoting continues:
There is no reason whatsoever why we should have to pay 24 cents a gallon for gas in British Columbia when the American troller can get his for 8 cents per gallon, besides he gets 2 cents per pound more for his fish. How' do you expect us trollers to be able to make things meet with this competition from the American troller, and all on account of the dominion regulations? Instead of helping conditions they are making them worse.
This is another long telegram to the same effect:
Do your best to have gas admitted on the free list to commercial fishermen. Otherwise the government will have fishermen on the bread line for next winter.
There is no concerted action in connection with these telegrams and letters; they are the spontaneous expression of men who are feeling the situation very keenly. What we want, to put it bluntly-I am not talking about the budget-is action on the part of the government by way of putting gasoline on the free list.
It is all very well, as I said a minute ago. to go to Washington. That is good and proper and may be highly successful two years from now, but two years will be consumed before results are obtained. A port tax might or might not work, but putting gas on the free list for commercial purposes is something concrete that we can do right now to keep thousands of men off the bread lines next winter. This is the situation not only on the west coast of Vancouver island about which I have

been speaking, but also in Skeena, my hon. friend's constituency, halfway up the coast of British Columbia where it was reported the other day the gill netters for spring salmon had to go out of business because they could not make any' money at 5 cents per pound for fish and 25 cents a gallon for gas. Who is going to keep them next winter? Is it not better to enable these men to earn their own living than to have to feed them? The other day the Prime Minister sent out his Minister of Labour, a very capable man, to British Columbia to look into the labour situation. He held meetings at Vancouver and Victoria, where a large number of the towns of that province were represented; I saw the names of many of them. Were the fishermen represented there? I did not notice it if they were, and yet the fishermen would be equal in number to the total inhabitants of three or four of what we call cities but what are known in the east as villages. But the fishermen were not represented at all. It is the duty of the Minister of Labour to return to Ottawa and report conditions to the government. When he comes to the fishing conditions, what has he to say? He has to say he does not know the first thing about them. The Minister of Labour held a meeting out there-I will not take time to go fully into it, but it was reported in the press-of the various municipalities. This was strictly a meeting-and I want to emphasize this lest I get stranded again on the rocks of the budget-for the purpose of dealing with unemployment and how to overcome it. Amongst others present was Colonel Villiers who controls practically all the public coal mines on Vancouver island. He made the statement that if he could get one dollar or SI .25 a ton bonus on coal, unemployment conditions among the miners on Vancouver island would disappear or at least be much helped. Without expressing any opinion about the budget at all-they were .discussing the matter from the point of view of unemployment-the Minister of Labour said there was a good deal of strength in that point of view and he would be pleased so to report to the government. That was without question by way of relieving unemployment. As much money as would be spent in keeping these men idle would keep the mines going and the men working. Surely to keep them employed would be the better proposition. The government should send a man out there who knows something about fishing conditions and who has an open mind.

Supply-Secretary oj Slate
I am not casting any reflection on the Minister of Labour, but he has no time and the government should send a man out who can find out what the situation is amongst the fishermen.
They received hardly any relief last winter because they had a little money and they endeavoured to scrape along, but they have nothing now and what will the situation be by November? The government is going to spend millions and we shall be glad to vote them for the relief of unemployment There is no criticism in that regard, but when the money is spent, what shall we have received for it? We shall have just the same situation next year-a large number of dissatisfied men, because people who do unemployment relief work with few days at small wages are always discontented. They can-n6t help being dissatisfied as to the past and hopeless as to the future. The human mind can encompass no more desperate or horrible situation than for a man or a woman or a community to be entirely hopeless as to the future, with nothing in sight, no opportunity to earn a living. What wonder is it if these men, as we are so pleased to say, become bolshevists! Would it not be better, instead of spending millions to keep these men more or less idle, to spend a few hundred thousand dollars to assist these men to help themselves? If you wish to know the blunt truth, I would say: Give us the $1.25 bonus to which we are entitled on that coal on Vancouver island and the miners will take care of themselves; remove the duty on gasoline and the fishermen will be able to earn a living. By the one policy you will find idleness, relief work, dissatisfaction, stagnation of business and everything of that sort; by the other, you will see work and encouragement, new life and hope for these men to go ahead in the desperate struggle they have been making in the past in trying to make a living, something they would far rather do even at a pinch, than be employed on unemployment relief work. Such a course will encourage them to renew the battle in an effort to bring about a return to normal conditions. Even if some of the profits of American capitalists interested in the oil business in Canada were shaved by ever so little -and it would not be very much, owing to the fact that the fishermen are not so very numerous-would it not be better to give the fishermen a chance by taking off the duty on gasoline than to give special unemployment relief? I commend the situation to the government.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.
